Jim Atkinson 
Named Dog Catcher 


Jack Rushton 
Feted by B.P.O. Elk 


Cloud 91 


Jim Atkinson was appointed the 
town dog catcher at 'the regular 
meeting of council held this week. 

Air. Atkinson will assume duties 
immediately and the town will post 
the 'local animal by-law to be en¬ 
forced by Air. Atkinson. 

Council will draft a new busi¬ 
ness licence by-law tor the town 
and wil eliminate the regular bus¬ 
iness tax. The by-law will be pre¬ 
pared for reading to be effective 
in the new year. 

Town secretary - treasurer, Clar¬ 
ence Schiie, will attend a second- 
year local government administra¬ 


tion course and assistant secre¬ 
tary John Kapalka wil attend his 
first year course. The courses are 
to be held this fall. 

The municipal inspectors report 
was read and indicated that all 
town business and affairs were be¬ 
ing conducted in an efficient man¬ 
ner. 

The Chinook Health Unit wiil 
hold a public meeting in Fort Alac- 
leod on the afternoon of Septem¬ 
ber 17th. Mayor John Holyk will 
represent Coleman. 

Council declared Octobre 15th a 
civic holiday. 


Jack Rushton, highly esteemed 
Coleman oldtimer was honored at 
the BPOE meeting Sept. 43 when 
charter member Bert Bond pres¬ 
ented him with a set of Elks cuff¬ 
links as a farewell gift. 

• In making the presentation Mr. 
Bond commended Air. Rushton for 
his 43 years membership in Che 
lodge, 28 years of which he assum¬ 
ed the duties of secretary. A social 
evening was 'held. 

Air. Rushton, or “Jack” as he is 


better known to his many friends in 
the district came to Coleman in 
1911 and worked for P. Burns Com¬ 
pany. He has many vivid recollect¬ 
ions of the old days in the ‘Pass 
mining camps. 

Jack also took an active interest 


St. John Ambulance Association for 
27 years. 

Mr. Rushton left town over the 
weekend for Edmonton where be 
will reside with a son George.

Blairmore Catholic cemetery.

allel itheir reaction to any other

is one specific menopausal symp¬ 
tom — the hot flush — which can 
and should be completely relieved 
by female sex hormones. These 
are usually a mixture of the hor¬ 
mones from the ovary; estrogen 
and progesterone.

decalcifying of the bones, which 
occur to a greater extent after the 
menopause. Women get shorter at 
this time. Until the menopause 
these changes are prevented by the 
sex hormones. The rationale of us¬ 
ing these sex 'hormones is to pre¬ 
vent these changes ever occuring, 
and 'there is a certain amount of 
evidence that this is possible. 

There is no doubt that these 
hormones increase the feeling of 
well-being and reduce fatigue. They 
have to be used in cycles, and af¬ 
ter each cycle menstruation oc¬ 
curs, which means that women 
may well be menstruating well in¬

ervision. The main disadvantage is

Strokes 'are usually caused by 
one of three varieties of disease 
processes, The Canadian Medical 
Association reports. The most com¬ 
mon of these is thrombosis, which 
is plugging of the arteries of the 
brain. Beyond the point of the plug¬ 
ging of 'the artery, the brain tissue 
dies. 

Symptoms of thrombosis include 
short episodes of weakness, dizz¬ 
iness, difficulty in seeing, numbness 
and tingling in the arms or bands. 
Relief from 'these symptoms some¬ 
times can be brought about by the 
use of blood-thinning agents known 
'as 'anticoagulants. These medicat¬ 
ions must be used with extreme 
caution by experienced physieans. 

Cerebral bemorrage, or bleeding 
into or around 'the brain, is the sec¬ 
ond most common cause of strokes. 
There are two varieties of cereb¬ 
ral bemorrage: one related to 'high 
blood pressure, which is often fatal 
and the other a rupture of a berry¬ 
like swelling where 'the arteries div¬ 
ide, which is less often fatal. Cereb¬ 
ral bemorrage often can be pre¬ 
vented by the control of 'high blood 
pressure. 

The 'third most common cause of 
strokes is 'the release of an embol¬ 
us or small blood clot into the cir¬ 
culation, which in turn plugs a 
brain 'artery, causing paralysis. 
These embolic strokes usually foll¬ 
ow changes in the heart valves 
brought about by rheumatic heart 
disease. Blood-thinning agents, fre¬ 
quently used by doctors oaring for 
patients with rheumatic heart dis¬ 
ease, sometimes reduce the fre¬ 
quency of embolic strokes. 

The C.M.A. -advises that many 
'Strokes can be prevented, or red¬ 
uced in severity, if 'treatment is 
commenced after the first symp¬ 
toms appear.
